newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Good food, free debates dominate Kuwait elections.
newsitem.headline: Good food, free debates dominate Kuwait elections.

text.p: Gourmet dinners, air-conditioned tents, pro-American Moslem traditionalists and free political debates unseen in any other Gulf Arab state are main themes of Kuwait's "democracy of the elite".
The small oil state will hold its second parliamentary election since the 1991 Gulf War on October 7, but only a seventh of the 700,000 citizens are allowed to vote.

Unlike most Moslem fundamentalists elsewhere, in Kuwait they are not anti-Western. They are openly grateful for a U.S.-led coalition that freed their country from Iraq's seven-month occupation in 1991.
"It is a fact of life. They (Americans) rushed to our help while some Arab and Moslem states took a disgraceful stand" by supporting Iraq, a leading Kuwaiti Islamist told Reuters.
While no political parties are officially allowed in Kuwait, to avoid rifts in the sensitive social balance, almost every political ideology is represented in the elections.

But Kuwaiti women, the most liberal in a conservative area, are banned from running or even voting although they are over 50 percent of Kuwaitis. In neighbouring Saudi Arabia they are not even allowed to drive.
Kuwaiti men born to Kuwaiti fathers can vote. Military and police personnel, Kuwaitis naturalised less than two decades ago and citizens less than 21 years old cannot vote.
Only some 100,000 can vote to pick 50 members for the next parliament from 250 candidates in the only direct Gulf Arab elections -- something Kuwaitis are proud to show off.

"Democracy in Kuwait is an isolated island," liberal MP Ahmad al-Rubai told hundreds who gathered for a rally by fellow university professor Abdul-Rida Asiri, followed by a free Shawarma meal -- sliced meat roasted on a rotating rod.
Kuwait's elections "are unique by Middle Eastern standards," said a senior Western diplomat. "They are exceptionally unique by Arabian Peninsula standards."
Whatever the outcome the crown prince, Sheikh Saad al- Abdulla al-Sabah, is expected to form and head the next cabinet even if parliament is again dominated by the opposition.
Ministers by law are ex-officio members of parliament.
No member of the ruling Sabah family is running but they are still expected to hold key cabinet portfolios like foreign affairs, defence and the interior ministry.

Rubai, who resigned as education minister on September 1 to seek re-election, warned a mainly Moslem Shi'ite crowd against internal strife between the various religious, political and tribal groups to avert a Lebanon-like civil war.

Constituents sat on carpets with their slippers and mobile telephones in front of them to listen to Asiri, a Shi'ite, and his Sunni backer Rubai, who called for "tolerance and acceptance of others" or else "the nation will become the victim".

After hours of speeches and discussions at election rallies about complex issues like the U.S. military presence in Kuwait and how to deal with much larger and stronger neighbours -- Iraq, Saudi Arabia and non-Arab Iran -- crowds gather late at night for free food offered by candidates.
"Food at some rallies is much better than others...The other day I went to one by a Moslem fundamentalist and he had catering by a five-star hotel," remarked a Kuwaiti official.
Two Kuwaiti newspapers run columns entitled "Tonight's dinner" and "What's on this evening", listing candidates speaking that night and political issues on the menu.
"I personally favour food to (election) promises," shrugged Jassem, 22, a Kuwaiti student getting his first chance to vote.
"Every night I eat the food of a different candidate."

Uniformed foreign waiters in bow ties roam election tents giving cold and hot drinks to crowds discussing claims of high- level corruption and public funds abuse prior to the 1992 restoration of parliament, which was dissolved in 1986.
Kuwaiti newspapers and streets are covered with election posters while empty lots are littered with dozens of huge tents.

In a well-to-do constituency, tents sit on each corner of a main street lined with similar tents offering a variety of lavish dinners in the back and political schools of thought in the air-conditioned front.
Outgoing deputies seeking re-election boast how parliament introduced watchdog panels and laws to monitor state spending and a foreign investment portfolio of some $35 billion.
"For the first time the Defence Ministry bows" and presents documents to parliament, said Islamist MP Ismail al-Shatti. "From whom military secrets are kept? The legislature? No (that will not be)."
Another Islamist candidate, MP Nasser al-Sanea, ended his rally with "good news". He said ministers had assured him that a newspaper story on Kuwait's first beauty contest was only a "rumour".
